summary.text: Take the counterexample \(n=33085221781504=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009\), where \(4409\) and \(458009\) are prime.  Multiplicativity of the divisor-sum function gives \(a(n)=2\sigma(n)-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)=2(32767)(4410)(458010)-(65519)(4411)(458011)=1\), although this \(n\) is neither exceptional value claimed.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\sigma(m)=\sum_{e\mid m}e
\]
denote the sum of the positive divisors of \(m\). The deficiency used in A296075 is
\[
\delta(m)=2m-\sigma(m),
\]
and hence the sequence is
\[
a(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\delta(d)=\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr).
\]
We will exhibit the positive integer
\[
N=33085221781504
\]
for which \(a(N)=1\), although \(N\) is neither \(1\) nor \(12\).

First, the factorization of the proposed counterexample is
\[
N=2^{14}\cdot 4409\cdot 458009.
\]
Indeed,
\[
4409\cdot458009=2019361681
\]
and
\[
16384\cdot2019361681=33085221781504.
\]
The two odd factors \(4409\) and \(458009\) are distinct primes. Here is a self-contained finite primality check.

We use the following standard form of Lucas's primality criterion. Suppose that the complete prime factorization of \(M-1\) is known and that an integer \(b\) satisfies
\[
b^{M-1}\equiv1\pmod M
\]
and, for every prime \(r\mid M-1\),
\[
\gcd\bigl(b^{(M-1)/r}-1,M\bigr)=1.
\]
Then \(M\) is prime. To see why, take any prime \(s\mid M\). The displayed conditions imply that the multiplicative order of \(b\) modulo \(s\) is divisible by every prime power occurring in \(M-1\), and therefore is divisible by \(M-1\). On the other hand, that order divides \(s-1\). Thus \(M-1\le s-1\), so \(s\ge M\). Since \(s\mid M\), this forces \(s=M\), proving that \(M\) is prime.

Starting with the evident primes \(2,3,5,7\), apply this criterion successively to \(19,29,229,57251,4409,458009\). The needed factorizations are
\[
\begin{aligned}
19-1&=2\cdot3^2,\\
29-1&=2^2\cdot7,\\
229-1&=2^2\cdot3\cdot19,\\
57251-1&=2\cdot5^3\cdot229,\\
4409-1&=2^3\cdot19\cdot29,\\
458009-1&=2^3\cdot57251.
\end{aligned}
\]
The following table records the modular computations. In each row, the indicated base \(b\) has \(b^{M-1}\equiv1\pmod M\). For each prime \(r\) in the factorization of \(M-1\), the table gives the residue of \(b^{(M-1)/r}\) modulo \(M\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
M&b&\text{prime }r\mid M-1&b^{(M-1)/r}\pmod M\\ \hline
19&2&2,3&18,7\\
29&2&2,7&28,16\\
229&6&2,3,19&228,134,165\\
57251&2&2,5,229&57250,55371,48088\\
4409&3&2,19,29&4408,209,3965\\
458009&3&2,57251&458008,6561
\end{array}
\]
Repeated squaring gives these residues. In every entry, the Euclidean algorithm gives
\[
\gcd(\text{listed residue}-1,M)=1.
\]
Thus Lucas's criterion applies row by row. In particular, \(4409\) and \(458009\) are prime. They are odd and distinct, so the three factors \(2^{14},4409,458009\) are pairwise coprime. Consequently every divisor of \(N\) has a unique form
\[
2^i4409^j458009^k,
\qquad 0\le i\le14,\quad j,k\in\{0,1\}.
\]
There are therefore \(15\cdot2\cdot2=60\) divisors.

We now evaluate the divisor-deficiency sum without having to list those sixty divisors individually. From the definition,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
 &=\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr)\\
 &=2\sum_{d\mid n}d-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\\
 &=2\sigma(n)-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d).
\end{aligned}
\]
The divisor-sum function is multiplicative on coprime arguments: if \(x\) and \(y\) are coprime, each divisor of \(xy\) is uniquely a product of a divisor of \(x\) and a divisor of \(y\), so
\[
\sigma(xy)=\sigma(x)\sigma(y).
\]
For a prime power,
\[
\sigma(p^e)=1+p+\cdots+p^e.
\]
It follows that
\[
\sigma(2^{14})=1+2+\cdots+2^{14}=2^{15}-1=32767,
\]
while primality of the odd factors gives
\[
\sigma(4409)=1+4409=4410,
\qquad
\sigma(458009)=1+458009=458010.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sigma(N)=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010.
\]

It remains to evaluate the second term, \(\sum_{d\mid N}\sigma(d)\). Using the unique divisor parametrization and multiplicativity of \(\sigma\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{d\mid N}\sigma(d)
&=\sum_{i=0}^{14}\sum_{j=0}^{1}\sum_{k=0}^{1}
  \sigma(2^i4409^j458009^k)\\
&=\sum_{i=0}^{14}\sum_{j=0}^{1}\sum_{k=0}^{1}
  \sigma(2^i)\sigma(4409^j)\sigma(458009^k)\\
&=\left(\sum_{i=0}^{14}\sigma(2^i)\right)
  \left(\sum_{j=0}^{1}\sigma(4409^j)\right)
  \left(\sum_{k=0}^{1}\sigma(458009^k)\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
For the two prime factors,
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{1}\sigma(4409^j)=\sigma(1)+\sigma(4409)=1+4410=4411
\]
and
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{1}\sigma(458009^k)=\sigma(1)+\sigma(458009)=1+458010=458011.
\]
For the powers of \(2\),
\[
\sigma(2^i)=2^{i+1}-1,
\]
so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=0}^{14}\sigma(2^i)
 &=\sum_{i=0}^{14}(2^{i+1}-1)\\
 &=(2+4+\cdots+2^{15})-15\\
 &=2(2^{15}-1)-15\\
 &=65534-15\\
 &=65519.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{d\mid N}\sigma(d)=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011.
\]

Substitution into the formula for \(a(N)\) gives
\[
a(N)=2\cdot32767\cdot4410\cdot458010
      -65519\cdot4411\cdot458011.
\]
The two products can be evaluated as follows:
\[
32767\cdot4410=144502470,
\]
so
\[
32767\cdot4410\cdot458010=66183576284700

dot
\]
(and thus twice this number is \(132367152569400\)); also
\[
65519\cdot4411=289004309
\]
and
\[
289004309\cdot458011=132367152569399.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(33085221781504)
 &=132367152569400-132367152569399\\
 &=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
(The isolated word “dot” in the preceding displayed calculation is only multiplication punctuation: the asserted equality is \(32767\cdot4410\cdot458010=66183576284700\).)

Finally,
\[
33085221781504\ne1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
33085221781504\ne12.
\]
Thus the implication \(a(n)=1\Rightarrow(n=1\text{ or }n=12)\) fails at \(n=33085221781504\). Hence it is false that, for every positive integer \(n\), \(a(n)=1\) if and only if \(n=1\) or \(n=12\).
